# OPTIMAL SOLUTION RANKS IN THE MAX-CUT SEMIDEFINITE RELAXATION AVINASH BHARDWAJ AND VISHNU NARAYANAN Abstract. For every _n_ and _r_ with \(1\le r\) and \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{r+1}{2}\le n\), we construct a connected unweighted graph on _n_ vertices whose Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation has a unique optimal solution of rank _r_. The main examples are the Kneser graphs _K(m,_2), whose unique optima have rank _m_-1. A six-vertex wheel supplies rank three, and attaching pendant vertices preserves both rank and uniqueness. For dense random graphs, we also prove a polynomial lower bound on the optimal rank. ### 1. Introduction The semidefinite relaxation of Max-Cut replaces the two signs defining a cut by unit vectors. This raises a natural question: how many dimensions can a graph force an optimal representation to use? We show that connected unweighted graphs can require every dimension allowed by the general rank bound, even with a unique optimal Gram matrix. Let _G_ be a graph on the vertex set [_n_] with symmetric nonnegative weight matrix _A_=(_aij_), zero diagonal, and Laplacian _L_=Diag(_A_**1**)-_A_. We denote the Goemans–Williamson relaxation [9] by SDP(_G_) and its optimal value by sdp(_G_): \(\mathrm{sdp}(G)=\mathrm{max}\big\{\frac{1}{4}\langle L,X\rangle:X\in\mathcal{E}_n\big\},\)
\(\mathcal{E}_n=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:X\unknown 0,\mathrm{diag}X=\mathbf{1}\},\) where E_n_ is the elliptope. A point of E_n_ is the Gram matrix of a family of unit vectors, and its rank is the dimension of the space they span. Rank one is the integral case: \(X\in\mathcal{E}_n\) has rank one exactly when \(X=xx^\top\) with \(x\in\{\pm 1\}^n\), a cut. Let _F(G_) be the set of optimal solutions of SDP(_G_), which is a face of E_n_, and define the _optimal rank_ \(\rho(G)=\mathrm{min}\{\mathrm{rank}X:X\in F(G)\}.\) Thus \(\rho(G)\) measures the dimension needed by the best optimal representation, and \(\rho(G)=1\) exactly when the relaxation is exact. Bhardwaj [4] shows that recognising exactness is NP-hard even for unweighted graphs. Optimal ranks have been studied from several angles [12, 15], and low-rank formulations also underlie heuristics for Max-Cut [5]. Here we ask how large \(\rho(G)\) can be as a function of the number of vertices. An upper bound on \(\rho(G)\) comes from general theory. _F(G_) is a nonempty compact face of E_n_, so it has an extreme point, which is an extreme point of E_n_; and by the theorem of Barvinok [2] and Pataki [18], an extreme point of a spectrahedron defined by _n_ linear equations has rank _r_ with \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{r+1}{2}\le n\). Thus an optimal solution of SDP(_G_) attains a rank satisfying this bound, and hence \(\rho(G)\le r_\mathrm{BP}(n):=\mathrm{max}\big\{r:\genfrac(){pt}{2}{r+1}{2}\le n\big\}=\big\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{8n+1}-1}{2}\big\rfloor.\) (1) The question we answer is whether equality in (1) is attained for every _n_, even by connected unweighted graphs. 2020 _Mathematics Subject Classification._ 90C22, 90C27, 05C50, 15B48. _Key words and phrases._ maximum cut, semidefinite programming, rank of optimal solutions, elliptope, Barvinok- Pataki bound, Kneser graphs.

<tbc>The distinction between arbitrary objectives and graph objectives is essential here. Extreme points of E_<sub>n</sub>_ exist at every rank permitted by (1) \[10, 13\]. Since every face of a spectrahedron is exposed \[19\], each is the unique optimum of a suitable linear functional. The same sharp rank bound appears in the extreme Gram dimension of Eisenberg-Nagy, Laurent and Varvitsiotis \[7\], where the objective coefficients on a fixed graph may be arbitrary real numbers. For an unweighted graph, the off-diagonal entries of its Laplacian belong to {0,-1}. Since diagonal terms contribute a constant on E_<sub>n</sub>_, it is this restriction on the off-diagonal coefficients that distinguishes our objectives. Our result realizes every admissible rank under this restriction, while also requiring connectivity and uniqueness.

The main construction uses Kneser graphs, familiar from graph coloring and Lovász’s work \[14\]. The graph _K(m,_2) has the two-element subsets of \[_m_\] as vertices, with two vertices adjacent exactly when the corresponding subsets are disjoint.

**Theorem 1.1.** _Let_ \(m\ge 5\) _and_ \(n=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{2}\)_. Then the relaxation_ SDP(_K(m,_2)) _has a unique optimal solution X_<sup>∗</sup>_, given by_

\(X_{ef}^*=\frac{m|e\cap f|-4}{2(m-2)}(e,f\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{[m]}{2})),\)

_and_ rank_X_<sup>∗</sup>=_m_-1=_r_<sub>BP</sub>(_n). In particular_ \(\rho(K(m,2))=r_\mathrm{BP}(n)\).

Explicitly, _X_<sup>∗</sup> is the Gram matrix obtained by assigning to the pair {_a,b_} the unit vector proportional to the centred indicator vector \(e_a+e_b-\frac{2}{m}\mathbf{1}\), where _e<sub>a</sub>_ is the _a_-th standard basis vector. Disjoint pairs have inner product \(-\frac{2}{m-2}\) and distinct overlapping pairs have inner product \(\frac{m-4}{2(m-2)}\). For _m_=5 this is the Petersen graph, whose unique optimal solution has rank 4=_r_<sub>BP</sub>(10).

The Kneser family skips rank three, because _K_(4,2) is a perfect matching. The wheel formed by joining a hub to all five vertices of a cycle supplies the missing rank, already on six vertices (Theorem 4.1). To reach any larger order, we attach pendant vertices: each new leaf receives the negative of its neighbour’s vector, preserving both the rank and the uniqueness of the optimum. These observations give a complete realization result.

**Theorem 1.2.** _For every_ \(n\ge 1\) _and every integer_ \(1\le r\le r_\mathrm{BP}(n)\)_, there is a connected unweighted graph on n vertices whose Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation has a unique optimal solution of rank r._

**Corollary 1.3.** _For every_ \(n\ge 1\)_, the maximum of_ \(\rho(G)\) _over connected unweighted graphs on n vertices equals r_<sub>BP</sub>(_n). The same maximum is obtained over all unweighted graphs, or over graphs with nonnegative real edge weights._

Thus every rank permitted by the general theory occurs as the rank of a unique optimum, even when the graph is required to be connected and all its edge weights are one.

The constructions also suggest a question about random graphs: must the dimension grow when the edges are chosen independently? For \(G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})\), where each pair is an edge independently with probability 1/2, we prove

\(\rho(G)\ge c\left(\frac{n}{(\mathrm{log}n)^3}\right)^{1/7}\)

with probability tending to one, for an absolute constant _c\>_0 (Theorem 6.1). Thus, with probability tending to one, every optimal representation of an Erdős-Rényi graph with edge probability 1/2 requires polynomially many dimensions. The proof compares the best objective value at bounded rank with a feasible matrix concentrated near the upper spectral edge. We also formulate a conjecture on the growth rate, motivated by the Gaussian spin-glass literature.

The proofs of the realization results follow a common pattern: first locate the range of every optimum, then use the diagonal equations to determine the Gram matrix. For the Kneser graphs, the classical Laplacian eigenvalue bound \[16, 6\] confines this range to the top Laplacian eigenspace.

<tbc>Van Dam and Sotirov \[20\] show that the spectral bound is attained for all walk-regular graphs, a class containing the Kneser graphs. Attaining the value alone does not determine the minimum optimal rank. We prove that the diagonal equations are independent on the relevant space of symmetric matrices, so the entire optimal face consists of one point. This is an application of the classical extremality criterion for correlation matrices \[10, 13\].

The centred-incidence representation is also central to the work of Godsil, Roberson, Rooney, Šámal and Varvitsiotis \[8\], who prove universal completability and unique vector colorability of Kneser graphs. Those problems prescribe or bound individual edge correlations; Max-Cut optimizes their sum. The difference is substantive: _K_<sub>4</sub> has a unique optimal vector coloring, represented by a regular tetrahedron, while its Max-Cut relaxation has both this rank-three optimum and rank- one optima coming from balanced cuts. For _K(m,_2), we establish uniqueness using the diagonal equations alone within the least adjacency eigenspace.

The wheel uses the same principle with the kernel of a dual slack matrix in place of the top Laplacian eigenspace. Finally, attaching a leaf preserves the optimal rank and uniqueness. This extension is a special case of the vertex-sum constructions in \[12\]. We collect the necessary facts in Section 2, prove the Kneser and wheel results in Sections 3 and 4, and assemble the construction proving Theorem 1.2 in Section 5. The final section gives a polynomial lower bound for random graphs and proposes a conjecture on the growth of their optimal rank.

## 2. The optimal face

We begin with the geometry shared by the two constructions. The dual of the relaxation is \(min\{\sum_iy_i:Diag(y)-\frac{1}{4}L\unknown 0\}\). The identity matrix is strictly feasible for the primal problem, so strong duality holds and the dual optimum is attained. If _S_ is an optimal dual slack, complementary slackness confines every optimum _X_ to \(rangeX\subseteq kerS\). A scalar diagonal choice gives the familiar eigenvalue bound.

**Lemma 2.1** (Eigenvalue bound \[16, 6\])**.** _Let_ \(\lambda=\lambda_{max}(L)\) _and let E be its eigenspace. For every_ \(X\in\mathcal{E}_n\) _we have_ \(\langle L,X\rangle\le n\lambda\)_, with equality if and only if_ \(rangeX\subseteq E\)_. If some_ \(X\in\mathcal{E}_n\) _satisfies_ \(rangeX\subseteq E\)_, then_ \(sdp(G)=\frac{n}{4}\lambda\) _and_

\(F(G)=\{X\in\mathcal{E}_n:rangeX\subseteq E\}.\)

_Proof._ \(\lambda I-L\unknown 0\) and \(X\unknown 0\) give \(\langle\lambda I-L,X\rangle\ge 0\), that is \(\langle L,X\rangle\le\lambda trX=n\lambda\). Equality holds if and only if \(\langle\lambda I-L,X\rangle=0\), which for two positive semidefinite matrices means \((\lambda I-L)X=0\), that is \(rangeX\subseteq E\). □

**Lemma 2.2** (Parametrising the face)**.** _Let_ \(E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) _be a subspace of dimension g, let_ \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times g}\) _have columns forming a basis of E, and let_ \(u_i^\top\) _be the i-th row of U. Then the map_ \(M\mapsto UMU^\top\) _is a rank-preserving bijection from_

\(\mathcal{M}=\{M\in Sym(\mathbb{R}^g):M\unknown 0,u_i^\top Mu_i=1(i\in[n])\}\)

_onto_ \(\{X\in\mathcal{E}_n:rangeX\subseteq E\}\).

_Proof._ A symmetric _X_ has \(rangeX\subseteq rangeU\) if and only if \(X=UMU^\top\) for a symmetric _M_, which is unique because _U_ has full column rank; for the same reason \(X\unknown 0\) if and only if \(M\unknown 0\), and rank_X_=rank_M_. The condition _X<sub>ii</sub>_=1 reads \(u_i^\top Mu_i=1\). □

In these coordinates, uniqueness becomes a question about linear equations: do the conditions \(u_i^\top Mu_i=1\) determine _M_? The following form of the correlation-matrix extremality criterion \[10, 13\] will be useful.

**Lemma 2.3** (Spanning forces a single point)**.** _In the setting of Lemma 2.2, suppose that the rank- one matrices_ \(u_iu_i^\top\), \(i\in[n]\)_, span_ Sym(R_<sup>g</sup>), and that_ M _contains a positive definite matrix M_<sub>0</sub>_. Then_ M={_M_<sub>0</sub>}_. If moreover E is the top eigenspace of L, then_ \(F(G)=\{UM_0U^\top\}\) _and_ \(\rho(G)=g\).

_Proof._ The equations \(\langle u_iu_i^\top,M\rangle=1\) are linear in _M_, and if the coefficient matrices span Sym(R_g_) they have at most one solution. The second statement follows from Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2. □ The converse holds whenever \(M_0\succ 0\): a nonzero symmetric matrix orthogonal to every \(u_iu_i^\top\) gives sufficiently small feasible perturbations of both signs. Thus uniqueness is equivalent to the absence of such a perturbation. In particular, \(n\ge\genfrac(){pt}{2}{g+1}{2}\) is necessary. Our constructions achieve equality before any pendant vertices are added. We will use two small graphs to start the construction. The graph _K_1 has the unique feasible matrix (1), of rank one. For the triangle _K_3, the objective of a Gram matrix of unit vectors _v_1_,v_2_,v_3 is \(\frac{1}{4}\left(9-\|v_1+v_2+v_3\|^2\right).\) Three unit vectors summing to zero attain the maximum. Taking inner products with each vector shows that all three off-diagonal entries of their Gram matrix are -1/2. Hence the optimum for _K_3 is unique and has rank two. The following extension lets us add vertices without changing the optimal rank. **Lemma 2.4.** _Let_ \(G'\) _be obtained from a graph G by adding a new vertex_ \(\ell\) _and a single edge_ \(v\ell\) _of weight one, where_ \(v\in V(G)\)_. Then_ \(\mathrm{sdp}(G')=\mathrm{sdp}(G)+1,\rho(G')=\rho(G).\) _If the optimal solution for G is unique, then so is the optimal solution for_ \(G'\). _Proof._ For any unit-vector representation of \(G'\), the old edges contribute at most sdp(_G_) and the new edge contributes \(\frac{1}{4}\|v_\ell-v_v\|^2\le 1\). Conversely, an optimal representation of _G_ extends by setting \(v_\ell=-v_v\), attaining sdp(_G_)+1 without increasing the rank. Every optimum for \(G'\) must therefore restrict to an optimum for _G_, which proves the equality of optimal ranks. Moreover, equality on the new edge forces \(v_\ell=-v_v\). All correlations involving the new vertex are consequently fixed by the old Gram matrix, proving the assertion about uniqueness. □ ## 3. The Kneser graphs We now construct the optimal representation and show that it is forced by the diagonal equations. Fix \(m\ge 5\), let _G=K(m,_2) and \(n=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{2}\). We write vertices as pairs _e_={_a,b_}, and _A_ for the adjacency matrix. The graph is regular of degree \(d=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m-2}{2}\), so _L=dI-A_ and the top Laplacian eigenspace is the least adjacency eigenspace. Let \(N\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) be the incidence matrix of pairs versus points, _Ne,a_=1 if \(a\in e\). Then \(N^\top N=(m-2)I+J\), where _J_ is the all-ones matrix, because a point lies in _m_-1 pairs and two distinct points lie in exactly one. Put \(E=\{Nf:f\in\mathbb{R}^m,\mathbf{1}^\top f=0\}.\) Since \(N^\top N=(m-2)I\) on \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\), the map \(f\mapsto Nf\) is injective there and dim_E=m_-1. **Lemma 3.1.** _The Laplacian L of K(m,_2) _has eigenvalue_ 0 _on_ span(**1**)_, eigenvalue d+m_-3 _on E, and eigenvalue d_-1 _on the orthogonal complement of_ \(\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{1})\oplus E\)_. In particular_ \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}(L)=d+m-3\) _and its eigenspace is exactly E._ _Proof._ For _x=Nf_ with \(\mathbf{1}^\top f=0\) we have _xab=fa+fb_, and \((Ax)_{ab}=\sum_{\{c,c^\prime\}\cap\{a,b\}=\varnothing}(f_c+f_{c^\prime})\)
\(=(m-3)\sum_{c\notin\{a,b\}}f_c=-(m-3)(f_a+f_b),\)

<tbc>because each \(c\notin\{a,b\}\) lies in _m_-3 pairs disjoint from {_a,b_}. So _Ax_=-(_m_-3)_x_ on _E_. The space \(\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{1})\oplus E\) is the range of _N_, since \(\mathbf{1}=N(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{1})\); its orthogonal complement is \(\mathrm{ker}N^\top=\{x:\sum_{b\neq a}x_{ab}=0\text{for all}a\}\). For such _x_ also \(\sum_ex_e=\frac{1}{2}\sum_a\sum_{b\neq a}x_{ab}=0\), so

\((Ax)_{ab}=\sum_ex_e-\sum_{b^\prime\neq a}x_{ab^\prime}-\sum_{a^\prime\neq b}x_{a^\prime b}+x_{ab}=x_{ab},\)

the last term correcting for the pair {_a,b_}, which is subtracted twice. Finally _A_**1**=_d_**1**. Hence _L=dI-A_ has the stated eigenvalues, and _d+m_-3_\>d_-1. □

_Proof of Theorem 1.1._ Let \(\pi=I-\frac{1}{m}J\) be the orthogonal projector of R_<sup>m</sup>_ onto \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\). By Lemma 3.1 and the identity \(N^\top N=(m-2)I\) on \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\), the orthogonal projector onto _E_ is \(P_E=\frac{1}{m-2}N\pi N^\top\), with entries

\((P_E)_{ef}=\frac{1}{m-2}\big(\mathbf{1}_e-\frac{2}{m}\mathbf{1}\big)^\top\big(\mathbf{1}_f-\frac{2}{m}\mathbf{1}\big)=\frac{|e\cap f|-\frac{4}{m}}{m-2},\)

where **1**_<sub>e</sub>=e<sub>a</sub>+e<sub>b</sub>_ is the indicator vector of _e_={_a,b_}. The matrix \(X^*=\frac{n}{m-1}P_E=\frac{m}{2}P_E\) has entries \(\frac{m|e\cap f|-4}{2(m-2)}\) ; its diagonal entries \((|e\cap f|=2)\) are 1, it is positive semidefinite, and its range is _E_. By Lemma 2.1, _X_<sup>∗</sup> is optimal and \(F(G)=\{X\in\mathcal{E}_n:\mathrm{range}X\subseteq E\}\).

It remains to show that every optimum equals _X_<sup>∗</sup>. By Lemma 2.3, it suffices to prove that the matrices \((\pi\mathbf{1}_e)(\pi\mathbf{1}_e)^\top\) span the symmetric operators on \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\). Indeed, the rows of _N_ restricted to this subspace are represented by \(\pi\mathbf{1}_e\), and the positive definite scalar operator \(M_0=\frac{m}{2(m-2)}I\) gives _X_<sup>∗</sup>.

Suppose a symmetric operator _M_ on \(\mathbf{1}^\perp\) is orthogonal to all these rank-one matrices. Extend it to a symmetric matrix \(\widetilde{M}\) on R_<sup>m</sup>_ by setting \(\widetilde{M}\mathbf{1}=0\). Orthogonality then reads

\(\widetilde{M}_{aa}+2\widetilde{M}_{ab}+\widetilde{M}_{bb}=0(a\neq b).\)

Let \(\delta_a=\widetilde{M}_{aa}\) and \(T=\sum_a\delta_a\). Summing over \(b\neq a\) and using \(\sum_{b\neq a}\widetilde{M}_{ab}=-\delta_a\) gives \((m-1)\delta_a-2\delta_a+(T-\delta_a)=0\), that is \((m-4)\delta_a+T=0\) for every _a_. Summing over _a_ gives (2_m_-4)_T_=0, so _T_=0, and then \(\delta_a=0\) for every _a_ because \(m\neq 4\). The displayed relation now gives \(\widetilde{M}_{ab}=0\) for \(a\neq b\), so _M_=0. By Lemma 2.3, _F(G_)={_X_<sup>∗</sup>} and \(\rho(G)=m-1\).

Finally 8_n_+1=4_m_<sup>2</sup>-4_m_+1=(2_m_-1)<sup>2</sup>, so _r_<sub>BP</sub>(_n_)=_m_-1 by (1). □

**Remark 3.2.** An alternative proof of the required nonsingularity follows from the entrywise square of _X_<sup>∗</sup>. The Kneser construction uses exactly \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{m}{2}=\mathrm{dimSym}(\mathbf{1}^\perp)\) vectors, so the diagonal system is square. Indeed, \((X_{ef}^*)^2=\langle u_eu_e^\top,u_fu_f^\top\rangle\) for its unit Gram vectors _u<sub>e</sub>_. Thus \(X^*\circ X^*\) is the Gram matrix of the coefficient matrices in the diagonal equations. With _B=J-I-A_, the adjacency matrix of the triangular graph, it equals \(I+\frac{(m-4)^2}{4(m-2)^2}B+\frac{4}{(m-2)^2}A\). On the three subspaces in Lemma 3.1, its eigenvalues are, respectively,

\(\frac{m}{2},\frac{m(m-4)^2}{4(m-2)^2},\frac{m^2}{2(m-2)^2}.\)

All are positive for \(m\ge 5\). At _m_=4 the middle eigenvalue vanishes: _K_(4,2) is a perfect matching and has \(\rho=1\), explaining the missing rank in the Kneser family.

**Remark 3.3.** The optimal value is \(\mathrm{sdp}(K(m,2))=\frac{n}{4}(d+m-3)=\frac{m^2(m-1)(m-3)}{16}\) .

## 4. Rank three

The Kneser family leaves one rank to account for. The triangle supplies rank two, but _K_(4,2) is a perfect matching and has an integral optimum. For rank three we turn to a familiar graph: the wheel consisting of a five-cycle and a hub adjacent to every cycle vertex. It has six vertices, the smallest order allowed by the Barvinok-Pataki bound for rank three.

**Theorem 4.1.** _Let H be the unweighted graph obtained by joining a new vertex to every vertex of C_5_. Then the Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation of H has a unique optimal solution of rank three and optimal value_ \((23+4\varphi)/4\)_, where_ \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2\). _Proof._ Write _h_ for the hub, label the cycle vertices 0_,...,_4 in cyclic order, and put \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2},b=\varphi+2,a=b^{-1},s=\sqrt{1-a^2}.\) Assign the hub the unit vector _uh_=(0,0,1) and assign the cycle vertices \(u_j=(scos\theta_j,ssin\theta_j,-a),\theta_j=\frac{4\pi j}{5}(0\le j\le 4).\) The five cycle vectors lie on a circle below the hub vector, with consecutive cycle vertices separated by an angle of \(4\pi/5\) around that circle. To see the choice of height, replace _a_ by \(t\in[0,1]\) in this representation. The sum of the edge inner products is \(\frac{5}{2}((\varphi+2)t^2-2t-\varphi)\), minimized at _t=a_. We next certify that this representation is optimal among all feasible Gram matrices. Let \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times 3}\) have the displayed rows. Its columns are independent, so \(X^*=UU^\top\) is feasible and has rank three. Let _AC_ be the adjacency matrix of _C_5 and consider, in the vertex order _h,_0_,...,_4, the matrix \(S=\left(\begin{array}{ c c } 5/b & \mathbf{1}^\top \\ \mathbf{1} & A_C+\varphi I \end{array}\right).\) The eigenvalues of _AC_ are \(2cos(2\pi k/5)\), \(0\le k\le 4\). On the nonconstant cycle eigenspaces, _S_ therefore has eigenvalues 0 and \(\sqrt{5}\), each twice. On the remaining subspace, with the constant cycle vector normalized to unit length, it is represented by \(\left(\begin{array}{ c c } 5/b & \sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & b \end{array}\right).\) This matrix has determinant zero and trace 5_/b+b_=5. Thus \(S\unknown 0\) and dimker_S_=3. The identity \(2cos(4\pi/5)=-\varphi\) shows that _S_ annihilates the first two columns of _U_. For the third column, the hub equation is 5_/b_-5_a_=0 and each cycle equation is \(1-(2+\varphi)a=0\). Hence _SU_=0 and ker_S_=range_U_. Let _AH_ be the adjacency matrix of _H_. Since _S_ and _AH_ have the same off-diagonal entries, every \(X\in\mathcal{E}_6\) satisfies \(\langle A_H,X\rangle=\langle S,X\rangle-5/b-5\varphi\ge-5/b-5\varphi.\) Equality holds for _X_∗ because _SU_=0. Minimizing \(\langle A_H,X\rangle\) is equivalent to maximizing the Max-Cut objective, so _X_∗ is optimal. For any optimum _X_, equality gives _SX_=0, and therefore \(rangeX\subseteq kerS=rangeU\). The graph has ten edges, so the optimal value is \(5+(5/b+5\varphi)/4=(23+4\varphi)/4\approx 7.368\). Its maximum cut has value 7: if _k_ cycle vertices lie opposite the hub, at most \(k+2min\{k,5-k\}\le 7\) edges cross the cut, and equality is attained by placing cycle vertices 0,2,4 opposite the hub. It remains to show that the diagonal equations allow no other optimum. By Lemma 2.2, write \(X=UMU^\top\) with \(M\in Sym(\mathbb{R}^3)\) positive semidefinite. The hub equation gives _M_33=1. The equation \(u_j^\top Mu_j=1\) at each cycle vertex becomes \(0=\frac{s^2}{2}(M_{11}+M_{22}-2)\)
\(+\frac{s^2}{2}(M_{11}-M_{22})cos(2\theta_j)+s^2M_{12}sin(2\theta_j)\)
\(-2asM_{13}cos\theta_j-2asM_{23}sin\theta_j.\) The five functions \(1,cos\theta,sin\theta,cos2\theta,sin2\theta\) are linearly independent when evaluated at the five angles \(\theta_j\). Indeed, multiplying a vanishing linear combination by \(e^{2i\theta}\) gives a polynomial of degree at

<tbc>most four with five distinct roots \(e^{i\theta_j}\). All five coefficients in the displayed equation must therefore vanish. Since _a,s\>_0, this gives _M_<sub>12</sub>=_M_<sub>13</sub>=_M_<sub>23</sub>=0 and _M_<sub>11</sub>=_M_<sub>22</sub>=1. Hence _M=I_, proving uniqueness. □

**Remark 4.2.** The wheel illustrates why it is useful to allow a general dual slack matrix. Its largest Laplacian eigenvalue is 6 and is simple: an eigenvector has entry -5 at the hub and entry 1 at every cycle vertex. No Gram matrix with unit diagonal can have its range in this eigenspace. The matrix _S_ in the proof instead uses a diagonal shift of the adjacency matrix tailored to the hub and the cycle vertices.

## 5. Realizing every rank

Each rank now has a connected unweighted example on the smallest possible number of vertices. Attaching leaves increases the order one vertex at a time while preserving the unique optimum and its rank.

_Proof of Theorem 1.2._ Let \(1\le r\le r_\mathrm{BP}(n)\), so \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{r+1}{2}\le n\). For _r_=1 start with _K_<sub>1</sub>, and for _r_=2 start with _K_<sub>3</sub>; as observed in Section 2, their optima are unique and have ranks one and two, respectively. For _r_=3 use the six-vertex wheel of Theorem 4.1. For \(r\ge 4\) use _K(r_+1,2), whose unique optimum has rank _r_ by Theorem 1.1.

These starting graphs are connected. For the Kneser graph, disjoint pairs are adjacent, while two distinct intersecting pairs have a common neighbour: since \(r+1\ge 5\), a two-element set can be chosen outside their union. Each starting graph has \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{r+1}{2}\) vertices. Attach \(n-\genfrac(){pt}{2}{r+1}{2}\) pendant vertices and apply Lemma 2.4 repeatedly. The resulting graph is connected and unweighted, and its optimum is unique and still has rank _r_. □

_Proof of Corollary 1.3._ The upper bound (1) applies to every graph under consideration. Theorem 1.2 with _r=r_<sub>BP</sub>(_n_) attains it in the smallest of the three classes, the connected unweighted graphs. □

Can the bound \(\rho(G)=r_\mathrm{BP}(n)\) be attained with a unique optimum by a 2-connected graph at every order \(n\ge 3\), or by a connected regular graph at every sufficiently large order?

## 6. Random graphs

The constructions above attain the largest possible optimal rank. We now ask what happens when the edges are chosen independently. The next result shows that a dense random graph forces every optimal representation to use a polynomially growing number of dimensions.

**Theorem 6.1.** _There is an absolute constant c\>_0 _such that, for_ \(G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})\),

\(\mathbb{P}\big\{\rho(G)\ge c\left(\frac{n}{(\mathrm{log}n)^3}\right)^{1/7}\big\}\longrightarrow 1.\)

The idea is to separate objective values: if every representation in at most _r_ dimensions performs worse than one feasible matrix, then every optimum has rank greater than _r_. After centering and scaling the adjacency matrix, we compare both values with the spectral edge 2. A Gaussian comparison produces a loss of order 1_/r_ at bounded rank, and a spectral construction comes closer to 2. The main work is to keep the errors small enough as _r_ grows.

_Proof of Theorem 6.1._ Let _A_ be the adjacency matrix and put

\(W=\frac{J-I-2A}{\sqrt{n}},F_n(X)=\langle W,X\rangle-\frac{\mathbf{1}^\top X\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt{n}}.\)

Centering removes the mean edge density: the off-diagonal entries of _W_ are independent symmetric signs divided by \(\sqrt{n}\), and _Wii_=0. The term involving **1** in _Fn_ accounts for the removed mean. The identity \(\langle A,X\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\big(\mathbf{1}^\top X\mathbf{1}-n-\sqrt{n}\langle W,X\rangle\big)\) shows that maximizing _Fn_ on E_n_ is equivalent to the Max-Cut relaxation. Define \(M_r(W)=max\{\langle W,X\rangle:X\in\mathcal{E}_n,rankX\le r\},\)
\(c_r=\frac{\mathbb{E}\|g\|_2}{\sqrt{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{r}}\frac{\Gamma((r+1)/2)}{\Gamma(r/2)},g\sim N(0,I_r).\) The Gaussian norm ratio satisfies 2_cr_=2-1/(2_r_)+_O(r_-2). Our two estimates are, with probability tending to one, \(\frac{M_r(W)}{n}\le 2c_r+C\big[r\sqrt{\frac{logn}{n}}+\frac{(rlogn)^{3/4}}{n^{1/4}}\big],\) (2) \(\frac{1}{n}max_{X\in\mathcal{E}_n}F_n(X)\ge 2-C_0n^{-1/5}.\) (3) The constants are absolute, and (2) holds for deterministic integer sequences \(1\le r\le\sqrt{n}\). The first estimate bounds all rank-_r_ representations; the second supplies a feasible competitor. We establish them in three steps, then compare the errors with the gap 1_/r_. ## 1. The low-rank gap for Gaussian entries. First replace _W_ by a matrix _B_ from the normalized Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE), whose independent upper-triangular entries are centered Gaussian with variances 1_/n_ off the diagonal and 2_/n_ on it. For a matrix \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) with unit rows \(u_i^\top\), set \(H_U=\langle B,UU^\top\rangle\) and \(Q_U=U^\top U/n\). The matrix _QU_ records how the row vectors are distributed among the _r_ coordinates. It satisfies \(Q_U\unknown 0\), tr_QU_=1, and \(\mathbb{E}H_UH_V=\frac{2}{n}\|U^\top V\|_F^2.\) The quadratic process _HU_ is easier to bound when compared with a process that is linear in the rows. Fix \(Q\unknown 0\) of trace one and independent _gi∼N_(0_,Ir_), and let \(Y_U=2\sum_ig_i^\top Q^{1/2}u_i\). Direct expansion gives \(\mathbb{E}(H_U-H_V)^2-\mathbb{E}(Y_U-Y_V)^2\)
\(=\frac{2}{n}\big(\|U^\top U-nQ\|_F^2+\|V^\top V-nQ\|_F^2\)
\(-2\|U^\top V-nQ\|_F^2\big).\) Thus the difference is at most \(4n\delta^2\) whenever _QU_ and _QV_ lie within Frobenius distance \(\delta\) of _Q_. To use this comparison, we discretize the row vectors and group configurations with nearby matrices _QU_. Use \(\delta=n^{-3}\) for both discretizations. A \(\delta\)-net of the unit sphere with at most \((3/\delta)^r\) points gives a row net N with \(log|\mathcal{N}|\le nrlog(3/\delta)\). Cover the trace-one positive semidefinite matrices by at most \(K=(1+2/\delta)^{r(r+1)/2}\) Frobenius balls of radius \(\delta\), centered in that set, and assign each \(U\in\mathcal{N}\) to one ball according to _QU_. Within a cell centered at _Q_, add to _YU_ independent Gaussian variables _ZU_ of variance \(2n\delta^2\). The increments of _YU+ZU_ dominate those of _HU_, so the Gaussian comparison inequality \[21, Theorem 7.2.11\] gives \(\mathbb{E}max_{U\text{in cell}}H_U\le 2n\mathbb{E}\sqrt{g^\top Qg}+2\delta\sqrt{nlog|\mathcal{N}|}\)
\(\le 2nc_r+C\delta n\sqrt{rlog(3/\delta)}.\)

Indeed, \(\mathbb{E}\sqrt{g^\top Qg}\) is symmetric and concave in the eigenvalues of _Q_, whose sum is one; it is maximized at _Q=I/r_. This is where the dimension-dependent gap enters. Each cell maximum is \(\sqrt{2n}\)-Lipschitz in the independent standard Gaussian coordinates generating _B_: the squared coefficient norm of _HU_ is \((2/n)\|UU^\top\|_F^2\le 2n\). Write _Zk_ for the maximum over the _k_-th nonempty cell. Gaussian concentration \[21, Theorem 5.2.2\] and a union bound give, for \(t\ge 0\), \(\mathbb{P}\big\{max_k(Z_k-\mathbb{E}Z_k)>t\big\}\le min\{1,Ke^{-c_1t^2/n}\}.\) Here _c_1_\>_0 is absolute, and no independence between the cell maxima is required. Integrating this bound, splitting the integral at \(\sqrt{(n/c_1)log(2K)}\), yields \(\mathbb{E}max_kZ_k\le max_k\mathbb{E}Z_k+C\sqrt{nlog(2K)}.\) Here _C_ is absolute. Since \(log(2K)\le Cr^2logn\), the contribution after division by _n_ is at most \(Cr\sqrt{logn/n}\). For any symmetric _T_, approximating each unit row within \(\delta\) changes \(\langle T,UU^\top\rangle\) by at most \(2n\delta\|T\|_\text{op}\). Since E∥_B_∥op=_O_(1), we obtain \(\frac{\mathbb{E}M_r(B)}{n}\le 2c_r+Cr\sqrt{\frac{logn}{n}}.\) (4) To compare with the zero-diagonal matrix _W_, put \(B^\circ=B-Diag(B_{11},\dots,B_{nn})\). Every feasible matrix has unit diagonal, so, pointwise, \(M_r(B)=M_r(B^\circ)+trB.\) As Etr_B_=0, these two maxima have the same expectation. The same identity holds when the maximum is restricted to the row net. Thus only the off-diagonal entries need to be replaced. ## 2. Replacing Gaussian entries by symmetric signs. We now transfer the estimate to the random graph. The maximum is not smooth in the matrix entries, so we first replace it by a logarithm of a sum of exponentials. This allows a Taylor expansion as entries are replaced one at a time, following the approach for random semidefinite programs in \[17\]. Taking expectation over the other entries and telescoping over the \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\) replacements gives total error at most \(C\beta^3/n\), with a constant independent of _r_. To pass to a probability bound, observe that changing one sign changes _Mr(W)/n_ by at most 4_n_-3/2. Matching the third moments is essential to this error estimate and is available here because the graph density is 1/2. ## 3. A feasible matrix near the spectral bound. We seek a positive semidefinite matrix concentrated on eigenvectors whose eigenvalues are close to 2. <tbc>The exponent 1/7 comes from balancing the comparison errors against the 1_/r_ gap; it need not describe the actual growth rate.

There is a more specific prediction suggested by the Gaussian infinite-component spin glass. Hastings [11] derived a ground-state dimension of order _n_<sup>2/5</sup>. Aspelmeier and Moore [1] supported this scaling numerically and gave an alternative argument balancing a finite-dimension energy correction of order 1_/r_ against a spectral correction of order (_r/n_)<sup>2/3</sup>. Balancing these two terms gives _r_ of order _n_<sup>2/5</sup>. Motivated by this prediction, we propose the following statement for unweighted random graphs.

**Conjecture 6.2.** If \(G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})\), then

\(\frac{log\rho(G)}{logn}\rightarrow^\mathbb{P}\frac{2}{5}.\)

The spin-glass calculations motivate this conjecture but do not establish it for the graph model. In particular, agreement of leading optimal values does not imply agreement of exact optimal ranks. Theorem 6.1 supplies a polynomial lower bound; even an upper bound \(\rho(G)=o(\sqrt{n})\) with probability tending to one remains open here.
